last_transition_reason: The proof correctly expands both q-binomial coefficients from the stated definition, splits the numerator product for r=k at k=l+m, simplifies the ratio, and reindexes/cancels factors to obtain exactly ∏_{i=1}^m (1-q^(l+d+i))/(1-q^(l+i)). The m=0 case is handled separately and correctly. No semantic drift or illegal dependency use is present.
latest_nl_proof: Interpret all expressions as formal rational functions in q. Since 0 <= l <= k <= n/2, we have n >= 0, so n/2 <= n and hence 0 <= l <= k <= n; therefore the stated definition applies to r = l and r = k. Set m = k-l and d = n-k-l. If m = 0, then k = l, so [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q = 1, and the right-hand side is the empty product, which is 1 by convention. Now assume m > 0. Then k = l+m. Using the definition for r = k and splitting the product after the first m terms, we get [n choose k]_q = prod_{j=1}^{l+m} ((1-q^(n-(l+m)+j))/(1-q^j)) = (prod_{j=1}^m ((1-q^(n-k+j))/(1-q^j))) (prod_{s=1}^l ((1-q^(n-k+m+s))/(1-q^(m+s)))). Since n-k+m = n-l, this becomes [n choose k]_q = (prod_{j=1}^m ((1-q^(n-k+j))/(1-q^j))) (prod_{s=1}^l ((1-q^(n-l+s))/(1-q^(m+s)))). Also, by the definition with r = l, [n choose l]_q = prod_{s=1}^l ((1-q^(n-l+s))/(1-q^s)). Therefore [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q = (prod_{j=1}^m ((1-q^(n-k+j))/(1-q^j))) (prod_{s=1}^l ((1-q^s)/(1-q^(m+s)))). Multiplying the two products together gives [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q = (prod_{j=1}^m (1-q^(n-k+j)))(prod_{s=1}^l (1-q^s)) / ((prod_{j=1}^m (1-q^j))(prod_{s=1}^l (1-q^(m+s)))). But (prod_{j=1}^m (1-q^j))(prod_{s=1}^l (1-q^(m+s))) = prod_{u=1}^{m+l} (1-q^u), and this equals (prod_{u=1}^l (1-q^u))(prod_{i=1}^m (1-q^(l+i))). Hence the factor prod_{u=1}^l (1-q^u) cancels, leaving [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q = prod_{i=1}^m ((1-q^(n-k+i))/(1-q^(l+i))). Finally, n-k = l+d because d = n-k-l, so [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q = prod_{i=1}^m ((1-q^(l+d+i))/(1-q^(l+i))), which is exactly the claimed identity. When m = 0 this is the empty product 1, as already noted.
role_in_parent: Rewrites the reduced quotient as a shifted interval ratio F_{b,m,d}(q).
statement_nl: For integers n, k, and l with 0 <= l <= k <= n/2, define [n choose r]_q := product_{j=1}^r (1 - q^(n-r+j)) / (1 - q^j) for 0 <= r <= n, with the empty product equal to 1 when r = 0. Set m := k-l and d := n-k-l. Then [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q = product_{i=1}^m (1 - q^(l+d+i)) / (1 - q^(l+i)), where the product is interpreted as 1 when m = 0.

domain_restrictions: n, k, and l are integers
The ordering constraint 0 <= l <= k <= n/2 holds
Because k <= n/2 and l <= k, both m = k - l and d = n - k - l are nonnegative
The q-binomial coefficient is defined only for integers r with 0 <= r <= n
The empty product is taken to be 1 when r = 0
The final product is taken to be 1 when m = 0
If the displayed product is interpreted numerically, the denominators 1 minus q to a power must be nonzero; otherwise the expression is intended formally or as a polynomial identity
The statement does not specify a numeric field for q, so q is treated as an implicit parameter or indeterminate
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every integer triple n, k, l satisfying 0 <= l <= k <= n/2, if m is k minus l and d is n minus k minus l, then the ratio of the q-binomial coefficient of n choose k to the q-binomial coefficient of n choose l equals the product from i equals 1 to m of (1 minus q raised to l plus d plus i) divided by (1 minus q raised to l plus i), with the convention that the product is 1 when m is 0.
